title: The king's offer
hookLine: in Rajagaha King Bimbisara offers him wealth; he declines (Sn 3.1), and later tradition adds his promise to return if he finds the way

cards: Rajagaha, capital of the kingdom of Magadha. A stranger with a shaved head walks from house to house with a bowl, eyes lowered, taking whatever is put in it.
From his palace, King Bimbisara sees him, and something in the way this man walks makes the king send messengers after him. Turning down something bad is easy.
Turning down something good, more money, a promotion, a place in someone's big plans, is a different kind of hard. That's what's coming on a hillside outside the city.

teach.h: A POEM IN THE SUTTA NIPATA.
teach.b: This scene is in the Pali canon itself, in a poem in the Sutta Nipata called the Going Forth. The king sees that this beggar is no ordinary beggar.

He walks mindfully, the poem says, eyes down, looking only a yoke's length ahead. The messengers find him on a hill outside the city, eating his alms food, and the king comes out in his chariot to meet him.
Then the offer. You're young, you're clearly of noble birth.

teach.h: WEALTH, AN ARMY — AND A NO.
teach.b: Come and lead my army. Take wealth, and enjoy it. The wanderer answers calmly.

He tells the king where he comes from: a people of the Himalayan foothills, the Sakyans. He didn't leave home looking for pleasures, he says. He's seen the danger in them, and he sees safety in letting them go.
I'm going to strive. That's where my heart is. The poem ends there.
The later commentaries add one more exchange, and it's the one people remember.
The king says: then when you find what you're looking for, come back here first and teach me. And the wanderer promises he will. Tradition says he kept that promise, and the story will get there.
What the scene shows is a no that isn't rude, bitter or proud. He declines a kingdom, kindly, and leaves the door open.
A promise to come back says: this no isn't about you. It's about the road.

how: Buddhists remember King Bimbisara as one of the Buddha's great lay supporters, and the Pabbajja Sutta, the poem of this meeting, is still recited and studied as an early account of the going forth.

o: the king of Magadha who offered him an army
a rival prince who wanted Magadha's throne
the general who led Magadha's royal army

games.q: who's in the king's offer — tap the pairs.

s: the meeting with Bimbisara is only in late legends
it's in the Pabbajja Sutta, a poem in the Sutta Nipata, in the Pali canon.
the promise to come back comes from the commentaries
the poem ends with his no; the commentaries add the promise.
the wanderer took the army but not the wealth
he declined both. he went to strive.

games.q: a king offers you wealth and command of his army. you're young, broke and sleeping on a hillside. what do you say?
o: no, kindly: I'm going to strive.
not now, but maybe in a year.
games.why: he declines. he left home not for pleasure but to strive. in the commentaries, the king asks him to come back first when he finds the way, and he promises.

practice: Think of something you've been offered lately that you don't really want: an invitation, a task, one more commitment, a second helping.

Picture declining it the way the wanderer did, calm and warm, without a long excuse, and feel in the body what a kind no is like: not a wall, an open hand. If it helps, try the words silently: thank you, not this time.

wordCard.voice: Bimbisara. The king of Magadha who offered the wanderer wealth and an army; he declined, and in the later telling, promised to come back.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the king of Magadha, who ruled from Rajagaha.

carryVoice: Your line: a promise to come back. A kingdom refused, and a friendship kept open. See you tomorrow.
